title: Kamario Taylor injury: LSU, Lane Kiffin given layup in CFP chase with star QB doubtful - CBS Sports
description: With Taylor and star RB Fluff Bothwell doubtful, the Tigers have an unexpected break to revive their playoff hope
body:
With Taylor and star RB Fluff Bothwell doubtful, the Tigers have an unexpected break to revive their playoff hopes before brutal matchups against Alabama, Texas and Tennessee
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 16, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:48 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        If LSU is going to squirm its way back into the College Football Playoff conversation following a 4-2 start and salvage an uninspired start to Lane Kiffin's coaching tenure, it's going to need good fortune and better football.Whether the No. 22 Tigers will play good football when they host No. 16 Mississippi State on Saturday is to be determined, but LSU is undoubtedly beginning the second half of its season with some good fortune. With Bulldogs star quarterback Kamario Taylor and top rusher Fluff Bothwell both listed as doubtful on Friday night's SEC student-athlete availability report, the Tigers appear to have been handed a layup.Taking advantage of it will be critical for a Tigers team that still plays No. 6 Alabama, No. 7 Texas and No. 14 Tennessee. After opening as a 10.5-point favorite amid uncertainty over Taylor's status, the Tigers are now favored by 17. With Mississippi State's breakout star likely to be sidelined by a foot injury that he suffered in a Week 5 loss to Alabama, the Bulldogs have lost their bite.The expected absence of Bothwell will only make life harder on Mississippi State's offense as it potentially navigates life without Taylor, who ranks No. 5 nationally in total offense per game at 321.8 yards.
Turning the page for LSUMississippi State's hobbled status gives the Tigers a great chance to start anew in the second half of the season after road losses to Ole Miss and Kentucky sullied the beginning of Kiffin's highly anticipated first season. While conventional wisdom suggests the Tigers need to win out and finish 10-2 to reach the CFP, there may still be some wiggle room.If the Tigers finish 9-3, they will have an 84.9% chance of reaching the CFP, according to the CBS Sports College Football Playoff Forecaster. In that scenario, they would need to go 5-1 overall and 3-1 against the four teams remaining on their schedule who are currently ranked in the top 20 of the AP poll. Three of those four top-20 games are at home, including Saturday's tilt against Mississippi State.Such an outcome is squarely within the realm of possibility for an LSU team that flashed its high-end potential in dominant victories over the likes of Clemson and Texas A&M. 
Getting to 9-3 or 10-2 will require cleaner play on both sides of the football for LSU. Turnovers have been a recurring issue for the Tigers, who are tied for 117th with 10 giveaways. The defense has been inconsistent, allowing fewer than 200 yards in each of LSU's four wins and 400+ yards in the two losses.But the idea of the Tigers figuring things out in the season's second half isn't outlandish. Flashes of potency have been there, even during its losses. LSU averaged 5.8 yards per play against Kentucky and racked up 26 first downs. The Tigers also scored 17 unanswered on Ole Miss in the second half before faltering late. Where Mississippi State will turnAfter Taylor, Mississippi State's second quarterback is listed as redshirt freshman Parker "Billy" Puckett" or fifth-year player AJ Swann. Puckett, a formerly unranked in-state prospect, has handled second-team snaps for the Bulldogs so far this season, completing 8 of 14 passes for 89 yards.
Swann is a former Vanderbilt starter who spent the 2024 season at LSU before transferring to Appalachian State last year. Now on his fourth school in five years — and third SEC program — he brings some experience to the position.But there's no replacing Taylor, who carried the Bulldogs to a 4-0 start before Mississippi State took a 56-23 loss against Alabama. He appeared to suffer the foot injury late in that defeat. Even after a bye week, it remains an issue.Former Georgia, Arizona State and Sacramento State quarterback Jaden Rashada is also on the Mississippi State roster, though he was not listed on this week's depth chart.

        Saturday's like this one are why being a college football fan is so much fun. The Week 7 schedule is bursting at the seams with top-25 matchups and rivalry games all day.You know it's going to be a good Saturday on the gridiron when the first game of the day is a top-five clash between the defending national champions and No. 4 Ohio State. No. 5 Indiana hosts the Buckeyes in a rematch of the 2025 Big Ten Championship Game and a possible preview of this year's conference title tilt.After that, we get a classic rivalry matchup when No. 6 Alabama faces No. 14 Tennessee in Neyland Stadium. Coming off a heartbreaking loss to Georgia, the Crimson Tide are entering one of the more hostile atmospheres in the SEC. Can the Vols score enough to keep up with Keelon Russell and the Alabama offense? Sophomore George MacIntyre will be making his second start.The night window is headlined by a top-10 battle featuring No. 2 Notre Dame and No. 8 BYU. It's one of the few major tests on the Fighting Irish's schedule, and Provo isn't an easy place to play. Bear Bachmeier will likely have to answer the bell when Notre Dame forces him to throw.
With so many great games on TV this weekend, keeping up with every snap can be hard, so we've developed a guide to help you prioritize your viewership.The best gamesNo. 4 Ohio State at No. 5 Indiana -- 12 p.m. on Fox, Fubo (try for free): For the third consecutive season, these teams will meet in a top-five matchup. The Buckeyes and Hoosiers have split the first two, and the rubber match figures to be a thriller. Defending champion Indiana has reloaded in the transfer portal and is coming off a narrow escape on the road against Nebraska. Ohio State has likely the best player in the country with Jeremiah Smith torching secondaries at an alarming rate. Don't miss this one.No. 16 Mississippi State at No. 22 LSU -- 12 p.m. on ESPN, Fubo (try for free): Just to be transparent, if I knew Kamario Taylor was going to miss this game for Mississippi State, this matchup would not be in this section. That being the case, let's cross our fingers and hope Taylor can suit up because the Bulldogs are a very dangerous squad with their QB1. On the other side, Lane Kiffin has to be feeling at least a little pressure sitting at 4-2 with one of the most expensive rosters in the sport. How do the Tigers respond to a devastating loss at Kentucky?
No. 6 Alabama at No. 14 Tennessee -- 3:30 p.m. on ABC, Fubo (try for free): This will be worth watching for the uniform matchup alone. For the first time in decades, the Vols and Crimson Tide will both wear their home jerseys for The Third Saturday in October. On the field, this matchup has plenty of intrigue. The Tennessee defense has been exceptional thus far, but it hasn't faced a quarterback like Keelon Russell. Sophomore George MacIntyre will be making his second start for the Vols, and he'll have to grow up fast to ignite the offense.No. 13 Missouri at No. 9 Ole Miss -- 3:30 p.m. on SEC Network, Fubo (try for free): Austin Simmons returns to Oxford after losing his starting job to Trinidad Chambliss last season, but the ground game will be the focus here. Missouri can run the ball with the best of them, and Ole Miss has shown a penchant for stopping the run with the worst of them. The Rebels were better in that area against Vanderbilt last week, but consider the competition. This has potential to be a high-scoring and tightly contested affair.No. 2 Notre Dame at No. 8 BYU -- 7:30 p.m. on ABC, Fubo (try for free): We've got a slobberknocker in Provo on Saturday night. Notre Dame and BYU are both physical squads who can play some defense. The Irish don't exactly have a loaded schedule, so they can't afford more than one or two losses. This is one of the only games in which Notre Dame might get pushed this fall. The question for the Cougars is whether they can throw the football if and when the Irish go all-out to stop the run.
No. 18 Oklahoma State at No. 20 Houston -- 7:30 p.m. on Fox, Fubo (try for free): The Big 12 may be even more wide open than it looked coming into the season with Texas Tech's offense sputtering and BYU star LJ Martin out for a while.                 Stokes is the most naturally talented prospect in the draft. He's big and powerful with long arms, magnetic hands, and real playmaking ability. He's made steady strides with his skill set, creation, and shooting over the years, but scouts will be watching for continued progress this season.

body:
Fantasy football is about finding the right matchups. Week 6 is becoming one of the most difficult weeks of the season for lineup decisions. With four teams on bye, injuries piling up and several offenses struggling to find consistency Fantasy managers are being forced to make some choices. As we have already learned through five weeks, a player's name recognition or draft position does not always translate into a spot in your starting lineup.Take Jalen Hurts and Justin Herbert, for example. Both entered the season with Fantasy expectations but offensive struggles and difficult matchups make them tough to trust in Week 6. Meanwhile, players such as MarShawn Lloyd, Germie Bernard and Denzel Boston are emerging as intriguing starting options thanks to increased opportunities and favorable matchups.That is why looking beyond the box score is so important. Defensive schemes, pass-rush pressure, offensive line play and expected game scripts can make the difference between a Fantasy performance and a disappointing afternoon. Sometimes the smartest move is to sit a name in favor of a less‑established player with a clearer path to production.We will break down every Week 6 matchup. Identify the toughest start/sit decisions facing Fantasy managers. From players worth trusting to established stars who might belong on your bench, we'll examine matchups, opportunities and potential pitfalls to help you put together the strongest possible lineup.
Dave Richard's Week 6 rankings: Top 150 | QB | RB | WR | TE | K | DST

Bo Nix has an average depth of target higher than 5.4 yards downfield in just one game -- Week 2 against the Jaguars (8.6) when he uncorked six throws of over 15 air yards, half to Jaylen Waddle. Jacksonville played a lot of man-to-man coverage in that matchup, and since then, the Broncos have seen just the eighth-fewest plays of man coverage against them. That trend will continue as the Seahawks are famously known for playing a ton of zone coverage under Mike Macdonald (they currently rank first at an 89.8% zone coverage rate) and they're also excellent at getting pressure on the quarterback without blitzing much. These are bad factors for Nix, who is struggling to throw downfield at all, let alone with efficiency. Jaylen Waddle doesn't have any good receiving metrics this season against zone coverage and doesn't even have an end zone target through five weeks -- it's really hard to trust him against the Seattle scheme. R.J. Harvey actually has the highest target-per-route rate among Broncos players this season, but didn't catch many passes in Week 5 because Denver stayed close and was able to run the ball. Expect that script to flip and for Harvey to be decent in the passing game.MUST-START: Jaxon Smith-NjigbaSTART: Emanuel Wilson, Seahawks DST, Broncos DSTFLEX: Jaylen Waddle, R.J. Harvey (PPR flex)SIT: Sam Darnold, Bo Nix, Courtland Sutton, JK Dobbins, Cooper Kupp, AJ Barner, Evan Engram, Rashid Shaheed

Woody Marks is expected to handle the majority of touches for the Texans, but it's against a Jaguars run defense that improved its rush yards allowed average to 2.5 last week against the Eagles' backups. Despite last week's heroics against the Titans, Marks is among the least efficient runners in the league, ranking bottom-10 among qualifiers in yards per rush (3.5), rush yards after contact (2.51), and rate of runs gaining zero/negative yards (27.9%). Unquestionably, some of this is due to his offensive line's woes, but it figures to hamper him against the Jaguars' defensive front. Marks will need to stay productive in the passing game to help in Fantasy, where he's been about league average this year. The Jaguars aren't quite as solid against running backs through the air, giving up a modest 6.6 yards per catch but missing on average more than two tackles per game against the position. Marks' workload, including his reception work, is solely what places him in the low-end No. 2 RB category.The Texans have the third-lowest blitz rate but are top-12 in pass rush pressure rate with or without a blitz. They're expected to lean into their pass rush, especially against the left side of the Jaguars offensive line, where veteran Walker Little takes over for injured starter Anton Harrison. Little had two of his worst games last year against the Texans, as did Trevor Lawrence, who has one career game over 19 Fantasy points against DeMeco Ryans' Texans defense. Lawrence has been really shaky when pressured this year, throwing a catchable ball at a low 61% rate (41.7% completion rate), with a much lower yards per attempt and QB rating compared to when he's not pressured. And when he is pressured, his targets are spread almost evenly, at least on a per-route basis, by Parker Washington, his peripheral receivers and his running backs, none of whom have impressive yard per route run rates in this specific situation. Had Lawrence fared better under pressure this year, he'd be a decent starter, but because he hasn't, and his track record isn't particularly good against the Texans, and the Texans themselves have been pretty good since faltering against Josh Allen in Week 1, it's probably worth considering benching Lawrence and lowering expectations for his other pass-catchers.

Stroud, Marvin Harrison Jr., Brian Thomas Jr., Jaylin Noel, Jakobi Meyers, Dalton Schultz, Chris Rodriguez Jr.

The Bears definitely tried to get Rome Odunze the ball against the Packers zone-heavy defense, but aggressive throws by Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum were broken up or intercepted (including four headed Odunze's way and two toward Colston Loveland). Moreover, the Bears ditched their quick-game pass attack, which is guaranteed to happen again this week with Caleb Williams back under center. Williams notoriously holds the ball a little too long and then scrambles to keep plays alive, sometimes with spectacular results, sometimes not. It's the primary reason why his best-known pass-catchers struggled in the first two weeks of the year -- plays designed for them went elsewhere because of Williams' tendencies. It's also why Kalif Raymond became a thing because he would frequently catch Williams' attention on those broken plays. The Falcons are a low-blitz, high pass-rush rate defense, exactly the kind that will send Williams' feet moving quickly. Williams' completion and catchable throw rates tumble when he's pressured. It's only been two games, but it's been Raymond who has, frankly, dominated per-route efficiency among Bears pass-catchers when Williams has been pressured or has faced zone coverage (which the Falcons play a lot of). Raymond is their third receiver, and his role hasn't really changed with Williams out, even though his targets have dwindled with Bagent and Keenum at QB. Atlanta has allowed 11-plus PPR points to two wide receivers in each of their past four games, seven of whom saw at least nine targets. Three separate times, a Bears receiver has had more than seven targets in a game this year, and just once (Raymond in Week 1) with Williams.MUST-START: Bijan Robinson, Drake LondonSTART: Caleb Williams, D'Andre Swift, Falcons DST (low-end start)FLEX: Luther Burden III, Rome Odunze,SIT: Michael Penix Jr., Kalif Raymond (bye-week WR), Kyle Pitts, Colston Loveland, Brian Robinson Jr. (bye-week RB), Jahan Dotson, Roschon Johnson (unless Swift misses time), Bears DST

The Ravens stay true to playing zone coverage without blitzing much. If there ever was a week for them to change that, it's this one: Deshaun Watson's passing metrics sink like a stone in Lake Erie when he sees man coverage, gets pressured or is against a one-high safety look. The Jets went blitz-heavy last week and sacked Watson eight times, something the Ravens should try to replicate. The man coverage will come on some third downs, and the pressure should be consistent versus a banged-up offensive line. Denzel Boston and Harold Fannin Jr. are two of five Browns players who see a target when Watson's pressured between 13% and 20% of their routes, and with poor efficiency (0.94 yards per route for Fannin, 0.47 for Boston). But it's the zone coverage where Boston has a fighting chance because he's been more effective (2.6 yards per route run), even if his target rate is a few percentage points behind Fannin's. With a pass-heavy game script on deck, not to mention a number of receivers hurt or on bye, Boston shapes up as at least a low-end No. 2 Fantasy WR, especially after coach Todd Monken said this week he wants Watson to get the ball out quicker.

If there was ever a get-right opponent for Daniel Jones, this is it. The zone-heavy Titans have mustered the second-lowest pass rush pressure rate this season at 26.8%, dipping to 20% over their past two games. They don't blitz a lot and they're keen on playing with a single-high safety to better contain the run. Taylor will absolutely get plenty of work, but don't be surprised to see Jones do well off of play-action and perhaps overall against a defense that's let up at least 20 Fantasy points to three of the past four quarterbacks it's faced. Best of all, the single-high safety look has led Jones to target Josh Downs at nearly a 25% route run clip for 1.94 yards per route, both well ahead of Keenan Allen. This feels like a make-or-break week for Downs, who has struggled in part because Jones has struggled, but the matchup suggests good things for Indy's pass game.    MUST-START: Jonathan TaylorSTART: Tyler Warren, Carnell Tate (No. 2 PPR WR), Tony Pollard (low-end No. 2 RB), Colts DST (bye-week DST)FLEX: Josh Downs, Keenan Allen, Wan'Dale Robinson (low-end PPR flex)SIT: Daniel Jones, Cam Ward, Tyjae Spears, Calvin Ridley, Titans DST

There's no question that rookie David Bailey turned the corner (literally and figuratively) last week against the Browns, boosting the Jets' pass rush in a big way. The question is whether he can do it again versus a Patriots offensive line that found a way to limit Maxx Crosby's impact a week ago. I'd expect the Jets to lean into their blitz more, but I'm not convinced they'll dial up much man-to-man coverage outside of third down. They've played the second-most Cover-2 this year and have nearly played the same amount of Cover-3, making up just over half of their total defensive snaps. In those specific situations, we could see Maye take downfield shots to Efton Chism III and Kyle Williams, with Chism a target per route leader against Cover-2 and Cover-1 (their third-most-used scheme and their most-used man-to-man scheme). Williams hasn't run enough routes to be considered for Fantasy, but Chism carries value as a high-floor PPR flex, as does Hunter Henry, who has come alive over the past two weeks as a middle-field winner from Maye. MUST-START: Garrett WilsonSTART: Drake Maye, Rhamondre Stevenson, Braelon Allen, A.J. Brown, Patriots DSTFLEX: Romeo Doubs (low-end flex)SIT: Geno Smith, Hunter Henry (bye-week TE), Demario Douglas, Omar Cooper Jr., Kenyon Sadiq, Efton Chism III, Kyle Williams, Eli Raridon, Mason Taylor, Jets DST

New Orleans' defense couldn't get off the field last week, struggling to apply quick pass rush pressure on Kyler Murray and then failing to wrap him up before he scampered away or threw downfield. Jameis Winston isn't a runner, but he has been pretty decent at evading the pass rush and late last week unlocked the offense when they went into more no-huddle work in the fourth quarter. Malik Nabers has crushed the past two weeks on a huge 33.3% target share (Isaiah Likely's 30.9% isn't bad either) and should shine versus the heavy Cover-3 shell the Saints deploy. With time to throw and a solid-but-not-studly Saints secondary, I suspect Winston can take advantage of his third straight favorable matchup in a row. It's that Saints defense that allowed the Vikings to control the clock last week, limiting Tyler Shough and the Saints offense to just over 20 minutes and a season-low 43 plays (their previous low was 64 plays). 
Tyler Shough and the Saints offense were limited to just over 20 minutes and a season-low 43 plays (their previous low was 64 plays) last week. They should be in better position to get more plays this week, but there's evidence that the Giants defense is improving. They've blitzed at the second-highest rate in the two games since Brian Burns' injury, paying off last week with five sacks. When they blitz Shough, they won't just be following in the Vikings' footsteps but in the Falcons' too -- each of Shough's past two opponents came after him, and both kept him under 18 Fantasy points. Shough's passing numbers against pass rush pressure have faded to a 52.1% completion rate for 6.0 yards per attempt, two touchdowns, and a 70% catchable throw rate, all awful compared to when he's not pressured. And, Shough's rushing has withered over his past two games, perhaps because he doesn't want to aggravate a "banged up" left hand injury. I'd hesitate using Shough this week, and I might lower expectations a bit for Chris Olave also since his best numbers might only come when Shough isn't pressured, which has been the case on just 58% of his dropbacks since left tackle Kelvin Banks got hurt.MUST-START: Malik Nabers, Chris OlaveSTART: Jameis Winston, Isaiah Likely, Cam Skattebo, Juwan JohnsonFLEX: Devaughn VeleSIT: Tyler Shough (bye-week QB), Kendre Miller (bye-week RB), Alvin Kamara (bye-week RB), Darnell Mooney, Noah Fant, Giants DST, Saints DST

Much has been made of Philadelphia's struggling offense, and with Jalen Hurts ruled out for Week 6, the Eagles face even more uncertainty heading into their matchup with Carolina. Their pass defense hasn't been particularly impressive, either. Their once-ferocious pass rush has just six sacks through five games, and their 32.8% pass-rush pressure rate isn't helped by their low blitz rate. Bryce Young's worst moments this season have come when he's been pressured, but that might not happen too often this week, especially if right tackle Taylor Moton returns to fortify a rested offensive line. It also helps Young that the Eagles tend to play a defensive style similar to the Panthers unit he practices against, right down to the heavy Cover-3 look. Jalen Coker has led the Panthers with a 30.8% target-per-route-run rate and a ridiculous 4.46 yards per route run against Cover-3 (Tetairoa McMillan has a strong 21.6% rate and 2.51 yards per route average as well). I would expect them to take turns lining up away from top Eagles cornerback Quinyon Mitchell, who has played to the quarterback's left nearly all season. With Hurts sidelined, Philadelphia's offense could struggle to sustain drives, potentially creating additional opportunities for Carolina's playmakers.A review of Tanner McKee's preseason film -- 58 dropbacks in Sean Mannion's offense -- shows him as a competent processor of coverage but perhaps a little too gunshy to aggressively throw downfield. McKee ran the quick-game passing offense, got through reads quickly, was willing to move his feet, rarely held the ball too long and would throw to easily defined one-on-one situations when he had the time. However, McKee was definitely too willing to get the ball out quickly to short-area targets, was affected by pass rush pressure, didn't throw with velocity often and was off-target frequently when he did. The Panthers typically play a ton of Cover-3 (single-high safety), but their pass rush pressure rate got significantly better versus the Browns and Lions offensive lines in Weeks 3 and 4. They'll be rested and ready to play against an Eagles O-line down at least three starters from Week 1. So even though McKee had time on the field this preseason with Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Dameon Pierce and Carson Steele, it's tough to buy into him connecting with them or anyone else for massive gains, even DeVonta Smith. Maybe the best hope is for McKee to throw a bunch of short targets to Lemon, Dallas Goedert and the running backs -- players with a low average depth of target.

The Buccaneers have settled into a heavy zone coverage unit, often with a single-high safety, blitzing at the NFL's third-highest rate but struggling to do anything with it. Todd Bowles' bunch has zero sacks in their past two games, six on the season, and just a 27% pass rush pressure rate. This lack of a pass rush has had a weird effect -- quarterbacks are comfortable but only one QB has over 20 Fantasy points against the Bucs this year, and it was Deshaun Watson. Everyone else has been below 17.1 Fantasy points, including Dak Prescott, who threw 42 times and Joe Burrow, who threw 35 times. I know Germie Bernard got a real opportunity last week, and I don't love chasing rookie numbers, but he actually leads the Steelers pass-catchers in per-route target data against the blitz and is just as targeted on a per-route basis against single-high coverage as DK Metcalf. It's been clear this year that Metcalf tends to see a good dose of targets against single-high coverage, but as a slot receiver, Bernard should be in the act as well. MUST-START: Jaylen Warren, Bucky Irving,START: Emeka Egbuka, DK Metcalf, Pat Freiermuth (low-end TE), Steelers DSTFLEX: Germie BernardSIT: Aaron Rodgers (high-end No. 2 QB), Jalon Daniels, Chris Godwin, Cade Otton, Ted Hurst, Tez Johnson, Darnell Washington, Kenneth Gainwell, Buccaneers DST (bye-week DST)

Filtering out garbage time stats, the Cards are below league average in a bunch of categories, including rush EPA, RB rush yards per game (3.6), and rush yards before and after contact, plus they're in the bottom five in explosive rush rate with just three runs of 12-plus yards. Their beat-up offensive line and banged-up rookie rusher, whose snaps are being managed, are huge factors. They've also averaged 18.5 running back runs (excluding garbage time) over their four losses. The most likely game script is that the Rams build a lead on the Cardinals' weak defense and thus force Jacoby Brissett to throw at least 35 times, which he's done in 4 of 5 games this year and in both games against the Rams in 2025.Tyler Allgeier is a low-end start based on volume (he's averaged more PPR points per touch than Love this season anyway).  MUST-START: Matthew Stafford, Puka Nacua, Kyren Williams, Trey McBride, Davante AdamsSTART: Michael Wilson, Tyler Allgeier (low-end No. 2 PPR RB)FLEX: Kendrick Bourne (PPR flex)SIT: Jacoby Brissett (bye-week QB), Tyler Higbee (bye-week TE), Bam Knight, Rams DST, Cardinals DST

The first thing to know before you consider starting any Chargers running back is that the Chiefs run defense held the Colts, Dolphins and Raiders to 3.5 or fewer yards per rush each in their past three games. Of the collective 72 rushes those running backs had, 21 of them went for zero or negative yards. That's nearly 30% of all runs, the best mark among NFL defenses in that span. Only three touchdowns were scored, two by Jonathan Taylor, including one from 24 yards out. This is a nightmare matchup for a Chargers offense expected to play behind on the scoreboard with a depleted offensive line (though they may have found something in the run game in rookie tackle Travis Burke). The second thing to know is that the Chargers used three RBs almost equally in their past two games. Omarion Hampton has played the lowest percentage of snaps among the three but got the most touches each week (at least 11 per game). However, if you go off the film, it's Kimani Vidal who's had more impressive runs and played with a little more physicality than Hampton as of late, and Keaton Mitchell is still delivering in the passing game. When asked about Hampton's decreasing snaps this week, coach Jim Harbaugh said he was "fired up" whenever Hampton was on the field, then went out of his way to praise Vidal before mentioning Mitchell. You can't help but wonder if Vidal picks up more than single-digit touches given his improved play compared to Hampton. Between that and the matchup, it makes me nervous to start any of them in Fantasy.
After Rashee Rice came up gimpy following a reception very early on in Week 4, the Chiefs effectively had Jalen Royals replace Rice's snaps but it was Tyquan Thornton and Xavier Worthy who saw the most targets -- eight for Thornton and seven for Worthy, but Thornton left Week 4's game with a severe injury and is out for a long while. The knee-jerk reaction is to assume the Chiefs will lean on Travis Kelce and Worthy as their top options in the passing game; no one from Andy Reid to Patrick Mahomes to even offensive coordinator Eric Bienemy offered insight on any of the other Chiefs wideouts. That's because the Chiefs are deliberate with how they bring along their receivers, which is why they might have been fine having Royals play a lot in their last game but not see many targets (just two, neither of which were first-read throws, despite a 64% route rate). Worthy has been discussed as a short-area target option before and has an average depth of target of 7.0 or lower in three of four games (not against the Raiders). If he's going to continue seeing targets then a stat line like what we saw in Week 4 or even Week 2 is certainly in play. Will that change Saturday in Bloomington?Ohio State's Heisman Trophy frontrunner has 38 career touchdown catches, one short of the Big Ten record held by Michigan's Braylon Edwards. Smith broke a similar slump earlier this season against Texas, which had held him in check in two previous meetings, and picked up 164 yards (in a loss) in Week 2.No other team has held Smith scoreless more than once. He can end that drought — and break another record — Saturday when No. 4 Ohio State travels to No. 5 Indiana. The Hoosiers are slight underdogs despite winning 22 straight games and posting a perfect 19-0 record at home under Curt Cignetti.Week 7 promises to be a big one across the sport. It's the first weekend since 2018 with four matchups between AP Top 15 teams.
No. 6 Alabama heads to Knoxville after a loss to Georgia, which climbed to No. 1 this week. The Crimson Tide haven't dropped back-to-back regular-season games since 2007, Nick Saban's first season, a streak of 220 games. The home team has won the last five games in the rivalry known as the Third Saturday in October. No. 14 Tennessee spent the week sorting out its quarterback situation — George MacIntyre will start in place of the injured freshman Faizon Brandon.Elsewhere in the SEC, Austin Simmons returns to No. 9 Ole Miss, where he opened last season as the starter before an ankle injury opened the door for Trinidad Chambliss. Now, Simmons brings No. 13 Missouri to Oxford for a gigantic showdown.Then comes Provo at night, as No. 8 BYU hosts No. 2 Notre Dame in one of the biggest games in Cougars history. The Irish have won 16 straight games by double digits but enter Saturday with seven consecutive road losses against AP Top 10 teams. BYU hasn't beaten a top-two team since Ty Detmer stunned Miami in 1990.
Plenty can change in one week. Remember, Texas was No. 1 last week, and Florida was in the top 10 two weeks ago. Nothing is safe in college football.Here's how our experts see the big weekend unfolding.
